summary: Defines the /.well-known/ path prefix for well-known locations in selected URI schemes. It obsoletes RFC 5785, updates the URI schemes in RFC 7230 to reserve that space, and updates RFC 7595. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: A standard place on a website where programs can find certain files without guessing, like a reserved shelf in a library.

questions: how to register a well-known uri
subtitle: A reserved /.well-known/ path prefix so protocols can find site-wide metadata without trampling a site's own URLs.

tldr.problem: Applications often need to find site-wide information about an origin before making a request, but picking an ad hoc fixed location risks collisions with other applications and with the site's own resources.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8615 reserves the path prefix /.well-known/ for http, https, ws and wss URIs and sets up an IANA registry where each application registers a precise name under that prefix.
tldr.outcome: Applications can claim a registered, collision-free location. The RFC obsoletes RFC 5785 and is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 8615 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 5785 and updates RFC 7230 and RFC 7595.

sections.title: Why Well-Known Locations Exist
sections.content:
Some web applications need site-wide metadata about an origin before they make a request. The RFC gives two examples: the Robots Exclusion Protocol, which tells automated processes whether they may access resources, and the Platform for Privacy Preferences (P3P), which tells user agents how to find privacy policy.

Per-resource mechanisms such as HTTP header fields or WebDAV PROPFIND exist, but their perceived overhead in latency or deployment effort often rules them out. HTTP is also increasingly used as a base for non-Web protocols, which sometimes need to locate resources on a host.

The obvious fix is a designated well-known location. The drawback is that such locations can collide with each other and with resources the origin already has, and they usurp the origin's control over its own URI space. RFC 8615 reserves one prefix, /.well-known/, so that future specifications can register their use of it.
sections.eli5: Programs often need to ask a website a question about the whole site. If every program invented its own spot for the answer, they would bump into each other and into the website's own pages, so one shared spot is set aside.

sections.title: What a Well-Known URI Is
sections.content:
A well-known URI is a URI whose path begins with /.well-known/, provided that the scheme is explicitly defined to support well-known URIs. If an application registers the name example, its well-known URI on http://www.example.com/ is http://www.example.com/.well-known/example.

The RFC updates the http and https schemes to support this. Other schemes can update their own definitions; RFC 8307 does so for ws and wss. Well-known URIs are rooted at the top of the path: /.well-known/example is one, but /foo/.well-known/example is not.

The RFC defines neither how to work out which hostname to use for an application, nor the scope of the metadata found there. Each application must define both. It also defines no format or media type for the resource at /.well-known/ itself, and clients should not expect anything to exist there.
sections.eli5: The special shelf is always right at the front door, never in some back room. And the rules for what goes on each shelf are written by whoever uses it, not by this document.

sections.title: Rules for Registered Names
sections.content:
Applications that want a new well-known URI MUST register it. A registered name must match the segment-nz production in RFC 3986, which means it cannot contain a /. Names SHOULD be precise: grabbing a generic term is discouraged. The RFC suggests example-metadata or example.com-metadata rather than metadata.

At a minimum a registration points to a specification that defines the format and media types obtained from the URI, and the URI schemes it works with. If no schemes are given, http and https are assumed. Applications normally use the default port for the scheme; any alternative port MUST be stated explicitly. Registrations may also describe extra path components, query strings, fragment identifiers or protocol-specific details such as HTTP method handling.
sections.eli5: If you want a shelf, you have to sign up for it and give it a clear label like "pizza-menu", not just "stuff".

sections.title: The IANA Registries
sections.content:
The "Well-Known URIs" registry is run by IANA. Registration follows the Specification Required policy from RFC 8126, on the advice of one or more experts. A request includes at least a URI suffix, a change controller ("IETF" for Standards Track RFCs), the specification documents, and a status of permanent or provisional. Related information is optional.

Values defined by Standards Track RFCs and other open standards are permanent. Others can be permanent if the experts find them in use; otherwise they are provisional, and the experts can remove a provisional entry that is not in use. Third parties, including the experts, may register a widely deployed name that would not otherwise be registered in time, but it still needs a specification reference.

The RFC also adds a "Well-Known URI Support" field to the URI Schemes registry, with a dash as its default value. Initial non-empty values cover coap, coaps, their +tcp and +ws variants, http, https, ws and wss.
sections.eli5: A librarian keeps the list of shelves. Shelves backed by official standards are permanent, and ones nobody uses can be taken away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because a well-known location effectively represents the whole origin, operators should control who can write to it, especially when several entities share one origin. Web browsers can reach these resources, so content injected through a Cross-Site Scripting flaw could make arbitrary requests to them. Applications should not assume they are the only user of an origin's cookies, Web Storage or other capabilities.

Listed mitigations include encrypting sensitive information, using HttpOnly and Path on cookies, and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff. Other good practices are an application-specific media type, Content-Security-Policy, Referrer-Policy, and avoiding compression of sensitive data.

Applications must define the scope of what they find. Applying metadata from https://example.com/.well-known/example to https://www.example.com or even https://www.example.com:8000 assumes a relationship that may not exist. Using a well-known HTTPS URI to bootstrap an unrelated service such as email can flood web servers with requests that resemble a denial-of-service attack. Finally, some administrators may not know the directory exists, since operating systems often hide names beginning with a dot.
sections.eli5: Anyone who can put a note on the shared shelf can fool every visitor, so only trusted people should get to touch it, and each note should say exactly whose house it covers.
